problem: Hedge sharpened: source 'that event may be attributed to' became 'the cause will probably be'.
replacement: If the free institutions of America are ever destroyed, that may be attributed to the unlimited authority of the majority, which may at some future time drive the minorities to desperation and force them to resort to physical force. Anarchy will then be the result, but it will have been brought about by despotism.

In a state of society where lawyers are prevented from holding in the political world the rank they enjoy in private life, we may be sure they will be the foremost agents of revolution. But we must then ask whether the cause that leads them to innovate and destroy is accidental, or whether it belongs to some lasting purpose of theirs. It is true that lawyers chiefly contributed to the overthrow of the French monarchy in 1789. But it remains to be seen whether they acted that way because they had studied the laws, or because they were barred from taking part in the work of legislation.

problem: Awkward number shift: 'the American people are ... they' then 'the people's ... its love of novelty'.
replacement: The more we reflect on everything that happens in the United States, the more we will be persuaded that lawyers as a body form the most powerful counterpoise to the democratic element, if not the only one. In that country we see how well the legal profession is suited, by its strengths and even by its defects, to neutralize the vices inherent in popular government. When the American people is intoxicated by passion or swept away by the impetuosity of its ideas, it is checked and stopped by the almost invisible influence of its legal counselors. These counselors quietly set their aristocratic inclinations against its democratic instincts, their superstitious attachment to what is old against its love of novelty, their narrow views against its immense designs, and their habitual delay against its ardent impatience.

problem: Causal 'As the jury was first introduced ... it is not an easy task' split into two unconnected sentences, losing the logical link.
replacement: Since my subject has led me back to the administration of justice in the United States, I will not pass over this point without mentioning the institution of the jury. Trial by jury may be considered from two separate points of view, as a judicial institution and as a political one. If my present purpose were to inquire how far trial by jury (especially in civil cases) helps to secure the best administration of justice, I admit that its usefulness might be disputed. Because the jury was first introduced when society was in an uncivilized state and the courts were merely called on to decide questions of fact from the evidence, it is not an easy task to adapt it to the needs of a highly civilized community, where the mutual relations of men have multiplied to a surprising extent and have taken on the educated and intellectual character of the age. *b

problem: Footnote prose left verbatim in 1862 wording (offences, furnish, afford, non-responsibility); notes are to be modernized, shape kept.
replacement: e [ An important remark must, however, be made. Trial by jury undoubtedly gives the people a general control over the actions of citizens, but it does not provide the means of exercising this control in every case, or with absolute authority. When an absolute monarch has the right to try offenses through his representatives, the fate of the prisoner is, as it were, decided beforehand. But even if the people were predisposed to convict, the way the jury is composed and the fact that it is not held responsible would still offer some chances favorable to the protection of innocence.]

problem: Term drift: 'manners' (mœurs) kept in the sense of customs and habits of a people; style note requires 'customs'/'mores'.
replacement: I am so entirely convinced that the jury is above all a political institution that I still consider it in this light when it is applied in civil cases. Laws are always unstable unless they are founded on the customs of a nation. Customs are the only durable and resisting power in a people. When the jury is reserved for criminal offenses, the people see its action only occasionally, in certain particular cases. The ordinary course of life goes on without its interference, and it is considered an instrument, but not the only instrument, for obtaining justice. This is true all the more when the jury is applied only to certain criminal cases.

problem: Term drift: 'the manners of the English' (mœurs) should be 'customs'.
replacement: The institution of the jury, if confined to criminal cases, is always in danger. But once it is introduced into civil proceedings, it defies the attacks of time and of men. If it had been as easy to remove the jury from the customs of the English as from their laws, it would have perished under Henry VIII and Elizabeth, and the civil jury did in fact save the liberties of the country at that time. However the jury is applied, it cannot fail to have a powerful influence on the national character, but this influence is enormously increased when it is introduced into civil cases. The jury, and especially the jury in civil cases, serves to communicate the spirit of the judges to the minds of all the citizens, and this spirit, with the habits that go with it, is the soundest preparation for free institutions. It fills all classes with respect for the thing judged and with the idea of right. If these two elements are removed, the love of independence is reduced to a merely destructive passion. The jury teaches men to practice fairness, and every man learns to judge his neighbor as he would himself be judged. This is especially true of the jury in civil cases, because while the number of people who have reason to fear a criminal prosecution is small, everyone is liable to have a civil action brought against him. The jury teaches every man not to shrink from the responsibility of his own actions, and gives him that manly confidence without which political virtue cannot exist. It gives each citizen a kind of magistracy. It makes all of them feel the duties they are bound to discharge toward society and the part they take in the government. By obliging men to turn their attention to affairs that are not exclusively their own, it rubs off the individual egotism that is the rust of society.
